tldr: This study introduces realistic dynamic environments across all 40 LIBERO tasks, where objects continuously move and observations become stale due to inference latency, systematically uncovering tracking performance, execution strategies, and the impact of dynamic data training across various policies.
hero_caption: Overall overview of LIBERO-Dynamic: (a) The gap between real-world dynamic environments and conventional static simulations, (b) the evaluation loop synchronizing model inference latency with physical simulation time, and (c) the framework for cross-evaluating diverse policies, execution strategies, and training recipes.
overview:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-model-based robot control policies have shown remarkable progress. However, conventional simulation environments used to evaluate them often assume that target objects remain static and that policy inference is instantaneous (actions are decided with zero compute time). In the physical world, time keeps moving forward while the robot processes camera images and computes its next movement, meaning target objects keep traveling. As a result, by the time computation finishes and the robot begins to act, the observation upon which the action was planned has already become outdated (stale), introducing a severe discrepancy.

To address this challenge, the authors propose "LIBERO-Dynamic", an extension of all 40 tasks from the representative LIBERO benchmark into dynamic environments. By driving objects via contact friction from an invisible moving floor within the MuJoCo physics simulator, objects travel along three trajectory families across three speed tiers without breaking contact and grasping physics. Furthermore, physical simulation time advances continuously based on calibrated, model-specific inference latencies measured on real hardware, reproducing realistic delays where objects move while waiting for inference.

In this work, the authors built an automated pipeline to synthesize dynamic demonstration trajectories from static demonstrations, collecting 9,000 trajectories, and evaluated six representative policies under a unified protocol. The results revealed that faster object motion degrades the performance of all models. Moreover, the choice of execution strategy (how inference and execution overlap) and action horizon dramatically shifts the success rate. These findings were also confirmed in small-scale physical robot experiments, underscoring the critical need to co-design model architectures, training data, and execution timing for dynamic robot control.
contributions: Built "LIBERO-Dynamic", a dynamic manipulation benchmark linking continuous object motion and model-specific inference latency directly with physical simulation

Developed an online displacement compensation method to automatically convert verified static demonstrations into dynamic ones, generating a quality-filtered dataset of 9,000 dynamic trajectories across 40 tasks
Extensively evaluated and compared six modern policies, execution strategies (Sync, Async, RTC, VLASH), and action horizons under a unified set of conditions
Demonstrated that temporal conditioning (such as observation history frames) substantially boosts the effectiveness of fine-tuning on dynamic data
Confirmed that simulation findings regarding execution timing and action horizons translate directly to real-world robot dynamic tasks

sections.heading: From a Static World to a Moving One: Why Inference Latency Matters
sections.summary: Conventional robot evaluations assume static objects and instantaneous inference, failing to capture object motion during computation and observation staleness. This paper proposes a unified benchmark extending 40 LIBERO tasks with controlled object motion and calibrated inference latency.
sections.details:
Generalist robot policies are rapidly advancing, making reliable evaluation benchmarks essential for real-world deployment.

In conventional simulation evaluations, time has typically been treated as if it freezes while the robot receives observations and infers actions. If the target object is static, inference duration makes little difference. However, when objects are moving, the target has already moved away from the "past observation" that the predicted action was based on by the time computation finishes and execution begins. This forms a major gap between the physical world and simulation.

While some recent works address dynamic object manipulation, their task distributions, treatment of latency, and execution protocols vary widely, making it difficult to fairly evaluate what drives performance. To bridge this gap, this study introduces "LIBERO-Dynamic". By controlling object trajectory patterns and speeds and reflecting measured inference latencies as simulation steps, it provides a fair and reproducible platform for dynamic evaluation.

sections.heading: Foundation Models, Dynamic Benchmarks, and Latency-Aware Execution Techniques
sections.summary: This study sits at the intersection of modern VLAs, world models, dynamic manipulation simulation environments, and execution techniques designed to mitigate latency in action chunking.
sections.details:
Related work can be broadly organized into three areas.

### Robot Policies and Temporal Modeling
Recent policies include autoregressive models (such as OpenVLA), continuous diffusion or flow-matching models (such as $\pi_0$), latent world models (such as VLA-JEPA), and video prediction models (such as FastWAM). While incorporating observation histories or future predictions has been explored for dynamic environments, differing training datasets and execution procedures have hindered cross-architectural comparisons.

### Dynamic Manipulation Benchmarks
In contrast to standard static environments such as LIBERO and RLBench, several dynamic benchmarks have emerged, including robustness variants and dynamic manipulation benchmarks such as DOMINO, DOM, and ReflexBench. This work plays a complementary role by maintaining the exact goals of all 40 LIBERO tasks while strictly controlling speeds, trajectories, and calibrated inference latency, enabling direct comparisons of execution strategies and chunk lengths on equal footing.

### Action Chunking and Latency-Aware Execution
Predicting multiple action steps at once ("action chunking") produces smooth motions but introduces a trade-off between inference latency and feedback frequency. Several execution mechanisms have been proposed, such as asynchronous queues that overlap inference and execution (e.g., LeRobot), RTC (Real-Time Chunking) which conditions on past committed actions for smooth transitions, and VLASH which aligns predictions by forecasting the robot's future state during latency. This benchmark directly evaluates and compares these execution mechanisms.

sections.heading: Invisible Floors and Latency Simulation: How the Benchmark and Dataset Work
sections.summary: Objects are driven using invisible platforms via MuJoCo contact friction, advancing the simulation by measured inference latencies. Additionally, 9,000 dynamic demonstrations were synthesized by applying online compensation to static demonstrations.
sections.details:
The benchmark design and data generation pipeline consist of the following components.

### 3.1 Tasks, Motion Patterns, and Evaluation Scale
Dynamic elements were introduced across all four LIBERO suites (40 tasks in total). Three trajectory families were designed: linear back-and-forth (Linear), smooth curves (Catmull-Rom), and broken-line zigzags (Zigzag), each featuring 5 trajectory variants. With three speed tiers (0.03, 0.06, and 0.09 m/s), a single model configuration faces a large-scale evaluation set of $40 \times 3 \times 5 \times 3 = 1{,}800$ episodes.

### 3.2 Contact-Driven Motion and Continuous Physics Simulation
Directly updating object poses via teleportation disrupts physical interactions such as grasping and pushing. Instead, an "invisible rigid platform" is placed beneath each object, driving it purely through static friction. Once grasped and lifted by the robot, the object naturally detaches from the platform. The control frequency is set to $f_c = 20$ Hz (50 ms per step). Pre-measured GPU inference latency $\tau$ is quantized into discrete steps $D = \lceil \tau f_c \rceil$, and physical simulation time advances forward during the computation interval.

### 3.3 Synthesizing Dynamic Demonstrations from Static Demonstrations
Collecting dynamic teleoperations manually is resource-intensive. Therefore, an algorithm was developed to replay verified static demonstrations while compensating the end-effector target positions online based on the moving object's displacement. Contact phases such as grasping and releasing are detected automatically to smoothly blend position offsets nearby. This generated 9,000 quality-filtered dynamic trajectories.

### 3.4 and 3.5 Execution Protocols and Evaluation Metrics
Four execution protocols were compared: "Sync", where the robot halts during inference; "Async", where inference and execution overlap; "RTC", which blends with past committed actions; and "VLASH", which forecasts future states. In addition to standard task Success Rate (SR), metrics include time efficiency $E_T$, path length efficiency $E_P$, inference query efficiency $E_I$, and steady underflow, which quantifies how often the asynchronous queue runs empty and stalls the robot.

sections.heading: Speed, Execution Strategy, and Dynamic Data: Revealing True Policy Capabilities
sections.summary: Evaluating six pretrained models highlighted performance drops at higher speeds and the severe penalty of queue starvation in asynchronous execution. Fine-tuning with dynamic data and physical robot trials proved that temporal input is key to dynamic adaptation.
sections.details:
Thorough experiments were conducted with inference latencies calibrated and reproduced on an RTX 5090.

### 4.1 Cross-Policy Comparison in Dynamic Environments
Six policies trained on static data ($\pi_{0.5}$, $\pi_0$, VLA-JEPA, OpenVLA-OFT, FastWAM, and FastWAM-Joint) were evaluated under asynchronous execution. Overall success rates ranged widely from 27.3% to 57.8%, with the flow-matching $\pi_{0.5}$ achieving the top score (57.8%). Increasing object speed from 0.03 m/s to 0.09 m/s degraded performance across all models by 4.7 to 16.3 percentage points. Furthermore, ranking inversions occurred compared to static scores (e.g., between FastWAM and $\pi_0$), proving that static dexterity alone does not predict dynamic tracking capability.

### 4.2 Execution Strategies and Action Horizons
Fixing the weights of $\pi_{0.5}$, execution strategies were evaluated across action horizons. Under synchronous execution (Sync), attempting frequent replanning (small horizon $K$) caused the robot to halt for ~147 ms on every cycle, causing success rates to plunge (dropping 25.3 points at $K=2$ compared to 43.1% at $K=16$). Conversely, under asynchronous execution (Async), the best score of 48.4% was reached at $K=6$. While $K=1$ and $K=4$ suffered severe queue underflows (828 and 330 times per 1,000 steps) and collapsed, the optimal approach was sustaining the minimal queue length without underflow ($K=6$) while refreshing observations as frequently as possible.

### 4.3 Fine-Tuning with Dynamic Data
Policies were fine-tuned under three recipes: static-only, dynamic-only, and mixed data. While single-frame FastWAM-Joint improved by only 8.8 points with dynamic data, the history-conditioned FastWAM-Joint (taking 5 past video frames) leaped by 21.7 points, rising from 45.4% to 67.1%. Models with temporal observation histories absorbed dynamic demonstration motions far more effectively.

### 4.4 Real-Robot Validation
Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot evaluated four tasks: conveyor belt handoff, Whac-A-Mole, and cart tracking (smooth curve and zigzag). Consistent with simulation, Async outperformed RTC. In Whac-A-Mole, where timing is extremely critical, longer horizons increased failure rates. This confirms that execution timing is an equally decisive factor in physical reality.

sections.heading: Limitations: Deterministic Trajectories and Constant Latencies
sections.summary: To ensure reproducibility, object trajectories follow preset patterns and inference latency jitter is omitted. Furthermore, zero-shot generalization to completely unseen tasks remains to be verified.
sections.details:
The following limitations apply to this study:

- ### Fixed Trajectories and Latencies
To guarantee strict reproducibility across benchmarks, object motions follow pre-defined geometric trajectory families without random, unpredictable motions or sudden disturbances. Furthermore, inference latencies are fixed at empirical median values, leaving the impact of computational timing jitter in real systems for future work.
- ### Scope of Generalization Testing
Although training and evaluation strictly separate trajectory motion phases during fine-tuning, the underlying tasks and trajectories are shared. Consequently, the findings demonstrate adaptation to dynamic conditions, while zero-shot generalization to entirely new tasks or unseen motions remains to be explored.
- ### Scale of Real-Robot Experiments
Physical robot evaluations were conducted on a single hardware platform across four tasks. Broader testing across diverse manipulators and more demanding operating environments is left for future studies.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Toward a New Standard for Dynamic Robot Manipulation
sections.summary: LIBERO-Dynamic establishes an objective benchmark for dynamic manipulation by integrating continuous object motion and inference latency into simulation. It highlights the interplay between architecture, execution strategy, and training data, offering crucial guidance for future foundation models.
sections.details:
This paper presented "LIBERO-Dynamic", an extension across all 40 LIBERO tasks that moves objects while preserving contact physics and synchronizes model-specific inference latencies with physical simulation time. In addition, an automated synthesis pipeline produced 9,000 high-quality dynamic demonstrations, creating a rigorous foundation for both evaluation and training.

A key conclusion across experiments is that performing well in a dynamic world requires not just a capable model, but also careful co-design of inference and execution timing. Frequent feedback requires an action queue that avoids underflow, and extracting the full benefit of dynamic demonstrations demands temporal conditioning, such as observation histories. With open-sourced code and data, LIBERO-Dynamic is expected to serve as a standard platform for dynamic robot manipulation research.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind the Friction-Driven Contact Model and Dynamic Synthesis Algorithm
sections.summary: This section details the friction conditions preventing slippage on the contact platform, along with the algorithm that automatically identifies grasping and releasing phases to smoothly adjust end-effector paths.
sections.details:
The appendix provides mathematical and physical details behind benchmark validity and data synthesis.

### A.1 Benchmark Construction Details
Among the 40 tasks, 25 tasks include 2 to 3 independently moving objects, and 5 tasks involve articulated fixtures such as cabinet doors or stoves. Static friction between objects and the invisible platform is calibrated high enough so that objects track the platform without slip, even under sharp zigzag turns and at the maximum speed of 0.09 m/s.

### A.3 Online Static-to-Dynamic Demonstration Compensation
Using successful static demonstrations, gripper opening/closing states and object proximity are analyzed to automatically identify "Grasp" and "Release" phases. During dynamic replay, the relative end-effector pose in the object's local frame from the static demonstration is projected onto the moving object's current pose $(\tilde{p}_t^o, \tilde{R}_t^o)$. The resulting target displacement offset is weighted by the contact phase, smoothed via exponential smoothing, and clipped within threshold bounds, generating smooth dynamic tracking motions without violating simulator physics.

takeaways: Policies that excel in static benchmarks do not necessarily lead in dynamic environments, with clear ranking inversions observed between static and dynamic evaluations.
When replanning frequently in asynchronous execution (Async), determining the minimum action horizon that prevents action queue starvation (underflow) is the single most critical factor.
When fine-tuning on dynamic demonstrations, architectures with temporal conditioning (e.g., multi-frame observation histories) achieve substantially larger performance gains.
Unless real-world inference latency is synchronized with physical simulation time, simulation results cannot accurately predict real-world deployment performance.
limitations: Object motions are restricted to deterministic geometric trajectories, excluding sudden evasions or unpredictable random movements.
GPU inference latencies are treated as fixed median constants, omitting real-world processing jitter.
Fine-tuning evaluations share tasks and trajectory families across phase-split splits, leaving zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks unverified.
